creator: Scottish Aviation Ltd
description: Drawing of installation of co-ordinate meter, drawing number SA-DAK-80-13, one of a collection of drawings relating to luxury civilian conversions of military Douglas Dakota aircraft, produced by Scottish Aviation Limited for engineering work and manufacturing purposes, dated 25 July 1962
free-field-content:
One of a collection of drawings, produced by Scottish Aviation Limited for engineering work and manufacturing purposes, and used on various projects carried out by Scottish Aviation Limited.

Most of the drawings relate to SAL work done in the late 1940s to convert ex-military Douglas C-47 Dakota aircraft for civilian use, primarily by British European Airways. There are also a large number of technical drawings of the Scottish Aviation Scamp electric car plus drawings for Grumman Mallard conversion, Beech 18 G-ASUG conversion, Lockheed Constellation & Super Constellation, Douglas Skyraider for the Swedish Air Force, and McEwan-King seat locks.

description: Vertical boiler, known as a cross-tube boiler, used to drive a threshing mill and other farm machinery, with horizontal single cylinder stationery engine, with later governor, possibly Scottish, engine made in Portland, Connecticut, USA, c. 1850, boiler by Farrar, Newark, England, c. 1945 - 1950
description-original: ASBESTOS HAZARD, identified in 2009 Asbestos register. Stationary horizontal steam engine, used to drive a threshing mill and other farm machiner; single piston machine with flywheeland crankshaft; the boiler was used with the engine from 1958-1973; also an ordinary galvanised storage tank, chimney, various pipes to fit onto the boiler and sacks of material which is mixed with water to make a paste to insulate the boiler. Engine manufactured 1850, boiler manufactured in 1945.  E. Edwards note, 2012-01-12: (information from Alex Hayward) Vertical boiler, known as a cross-tube boiler.  The fire would be at the bottom of the boiler & the door through which it would be fed is clearly visible.  This is a basic steam boiler.  The internal tubes would be full of water in order to create the steam.  Date c. 1945-50 (the date was determined by the welded seam on the fire box).  This style of boiler was simple to make & therefore relatively cheap.  It only has a small footprint & is not too tall, so it was considered to be compact. They weren’t very economical, although the cross-tubes were intended to make it so. They would have been used in a variety of premises such as diaries, small factories & for driving steam cranes.  The maker’s name (Farrar of Newark) is marked on the safety valve.  The larger hole on the side of the boiler is known as a man-hole, this was to allow someone to either get their head through or if necessary for someone to climb inside (often an apprentice). The smaller holes were known as ‘mud-holes’, they allowed access to clean out the ‘mud’ from inside.  Each of these holes has a door, which have been located on a pallet near the boiler in building 11.  Each door was sealed with asbestos, though steam did leak through & cause rust around the joint.  The engine belonging to this boiler is c. 1850, it’s known as a horizontal single cylinder stationery engine.  It’s quite small apx. 10-12 brake horse power (BHP).  The governor states’ The Pickering, Portland, Conn. USA’.  AH said these were patented in 1862.  AH states the governor is a later addition to the engine. This is a British design, possibly Scottish.  AH & I discussed the possibility of this being put back into use, which I said I’d be happy for this to happen. However, the object should be kept in the collection.

description: Drawing of installation bush sight, drawing number SA-DAK-80-15 sheet 1 of 3, one of a collection of drawings relating to luxury civilian conversions of military Douglas Dakota aircraft, produced by Scottish Aviation Limited for engineering work and manufacturing purposes, dated 14 September 1962
free-field-content:
One of a collection of drawings, produced by Scottish Aviation Limited for engineering work and manufacturing purposes, and used on various projects carried out by Scottish Aviation Limited.

Most of the drawings relate to SAL work done in the late 1940s to convert ex-military Douglas C-47 Dakota aircraft for civilian use, primarily by British European Airways. There are also a large number of technical drawings of the Scottish Aviation Scamp electric car plus drawings for Grumman Mallard conversion, Beech 18 G-ASUG conversion, Lockheed Constellation & Super Constellation, Douglas Skyraider for the Swedish Air Force, and McEwan-King seat locks.
